name: The Periclean flowering of Athens
plain_explanation: In only a few decades a previously minor city produced tragedy, comedy, monumental architecture, sculpture, and history-writing that still shape Western culture, despite a tiny population by modern standards.
precise_definition: Russell's account of the concentrated burst of artistic and civic achievement in Athens under Pericles's leadership (down to his fall in 430 B.C.), financed by the transformed Delian League and enabled by relative internal political stability.
why_it_mattered: It set the material and cultural context in which Socrates matured and against which Plato's dialogues are set, and it illustrates Russell's recurring theme that cultural achievement depends on unstable political and economic conditions rather than emerging in a vacuum.
historical_origin: Grew out of Athens's leadership of Greek resistance to Persia and its conversion of a defensive alliance into an empire.
examples: Rebuilding of the Parthenon and the other Acropolis temples
The tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides
Pheidias's colossal statues of gods and goddesses
Herodotus's history of the Persian Wars, written from the Athenian point of view
influence_on_later_thinkers: Provided the setting Plato's dialogues later idealize as a lost aristocratic world of leisure and intellectual freedom.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Funded by imperial tribute and closely bound to Pericles's personal political ascendancy and to civic religion (temple-building).
